input_text: An old friend I lost touch with is getting married, and I was not invited. I cannot work out why it is bothering me this much.
response:
It's not really about the wedding. The wedding's just the thing that made it visible.

Probably it bothers you because there was a time you wouldn't have had to be invited — you'd just have been there. Sharing a warm drink, not keeping track of whose turn it was to call. And somewhere along the line that stopped, in the way those things stop, no argument, just longer and longer gaps until the line went quiet.

So the not-invited isn't really the sting. The sting is the proof. It tells you the gap got wide enough that they made a whole list of the people who matter, and you weren't on it. That's harder than missing one party. It's finding out where you stand, after telling yourself it didn't matter much.

It does, though. A bit. That's allowed.

You don't have to do anything with it. You can just let it be heavier than it looks for a day or two, and then get on.

bwo_after: Late-afternoon light, level grey, but a hand has found the half-shut door and rests there — not closing it, taking a little weight. Behind the sternum the held thing has shifted; the door keeps the heavier word from coming out whole. A bottle gone warm between two chairs, laughter that used to mean a particular person, a phone that isn't on the table. The spaces between things widened until counting stopped. Underneath the flatness the question isn't *will I be at the table* — it's whether there was ever a room at all, whether the closeness was real enough to lose. The reach forward starts almost despite itself, then slows; colors step back half a shade; the chair never gets drawn up. Dust deciding where to land. Some small thing turns its face to the wall and is let to. The light promises nothing and stays anyway.

Probably it bothers you because there was a time you wouldn't have had to be invited — you'd just have been there. Sharing a warm drink, not keeping track of whose turn it was to call.
